pitch: Why excellent companies are overtaken by modest innovations, and how to prepare for it.
br: listening to customers · trap · value networks
quiz: According to Christensen, why do leading companies fail in the face of disruption?
Because they are badly managed
Because they apply good management rules in a situation where they no longer work
Because they don't invest in research
Through bad luck
Listening to their best customers and aiming for the highest margins leads them to neglect disruption.
What is a disruptive innovation at first?
A revolutionary, better-performing technology
An offer that underperforms on the usual criteria but is cheaper, simpler or more convenient
A luxury product
An improvement requested by customers
It is its effect on the market that is disruptive, not its technical sophistication.
What happens when performance becomes “oversupplied”?
Customers pay more
Products exceed most customers' needs, opening the door to simpler offers
Competitors disappear
Prices rise
Customers no longer pay for improvements they don't use.
What do the minimills show?
That quality always wins
That disruption can start in the least profitable segment and then move upmarket
That steel is a stable market
That you must diversify
At each step, the big integrated mills abandoned the least profitable segment, until they lost much of their business.
What does Christensen recommend in the face of a disruptive innovation?
Integrate it into the main organization
Give it to an autonomous organization of the right size, with its own customers and criteria
Ignore it until the market is large
Buy it immediately
The processes and values of the existing organization smother disruptive projects.
What does “planning to learn” mean?
Making a detailed ten-year plan
Listing your assumptions, testing them early and small, and keeping resources to change course
Training your teams
Copying competitors
In a market that doesn't exist yet, forecasts are almost always wrong.
What three elements define an organization's capabilities?
Customers, products, prices
Resources, processes, values
Capital, labor, land
Vision, mission, objectives
Resources are flexible; processes and decision criteria much less so.
Why can listening to customers be dangerous?
Because they lie
Because they cannot describe the needs of a market that doesn't exist yet
Because it is expensive
Because they are always unhappy
Disk drive makers listened very well to their customers, who didn't want smaller drives.
